utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Ms. Dahl, to Mr. Seselj and to all the people in the courtroom. Before giving you the floor, Ms. Dahl, because I think you wanted to say something, let me say two things. First, Mr. Seselj, you have now available to you a fax and a telephone line. We're going to have a break at 10.00, and then you'll have somebody who's going to explain the way it works to you. We'll have a 30-minute break then because we were told we need at least 30 minutes for all this to be done. This is what I wanted to say first. Secondly, as to the time for the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, we discussed this matter among Judges and we can now tell you, Ms. Dahl, that you have already used up three hours. You get another two hours. You'll have five hours in all. So in the two hours remaining to you, if you wish to introduce new documents, please focus on them and focus on what is essential. This is what I wanted to tell you. You wanted to tell us something, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like to -- oops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We're in open session. I will give the floor to Mrs. Dahl for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to present the witness with his 89(F) statement from 2006 so that I can preserve the record in the event that we are permitted to appeal the decision on the Prosecution's consolidated motion regarding witness statements. There's prerequisites for the admission, and I'd like to begin by satisfying that. I wanted to like to let you know, in light of the discussion yesterday about using the statement, that I would be doing that. So I would like the registrar to bring up the 89(F) statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It's document number 07044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I oppose this attempt made by the Prosecution because this is not the statement that was written by Mr. Stoparic. This is a statement that was written by OTP officials and it was just handed over to him to sign. Now the Prosecution would like to suggest things in different ways, to lead a witness through the statement and to make him confirm what is stated there, while a witness should testify only extemporaneously unless he took notes during the course of the war. He should give answers from his own head, not on the basis of a statement taken by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... independently of what Mr. Seselj just said. When you -- at line 23 when you talked about the statement -- 89(F) statement I was wondering what you were talking about and what you were looking for exactly. Let me explain exactly. The Trial Chamber issued a decision according to which we would have a viva voce procedure. You're asking questions, the witness answers the questions. As a consequence of this, the statement is not admitted in the framework of this procedure. Of course later on you can submit a motion saying that in the interests of justice this statement should be admitted, but you can do this only afterwards. However, you are entitled, and I told you this yesterday, this is in accordance with the case law of the Appeals Chamber, you can submit a -- you can present the declaration -- the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can present the statement to the witness in order to refresh his memory. You may think that his memory is not very good and then in order to refresh his memory show him the statement and say, Look at paragraph X, you signed the document, you said it was accurate at the time, and I would now like to know whether you can give us explanations on this. Now, as far as I'm concerned, and I don't know exactly what my fellow Judges think regarding this issue because we did not consult, but as far as I'm concerned, it's out of the question that this statement be admitted according to Rule 89(F). This is my position. Of course you may show the statement to the witness telling him, On such and such year you said this and what would you say now. You can do this. This is as far as you can go. Now, regarding what Mr. Seselj says, the fact that he raises an objection and he's against the admission because the statement was made by the OTP, well, this is not enough. It is true that it is the investigator who drafted the statement, but the statement has been signed and by signing the document the witness certified and authentified what was in the statement. In any investigation the witness is told what -- is read back his statement in his own language. So this is my answer. Mrs. Dahl, you may display the statement on the screen and you may ask him your question relating to a specific paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would like to do is demonstrate the satisfaction of the prerequisites under Rule 92 ter (A)(iii) so that in the event we are permitted an interlocutory appeal of the decision that the requirements under the rule for admission of the document have been met while the witness is here and it's foundational questions that I want to put to him to demonstrate whether -- it's to preserve the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, let me answer. Article -- Rule 92 ter as it is was introduced during a plenary assembly at my request. I am the father, if I could say so, of this 92 ter rule, so I know about this. Now, regarding 92 ter (A), the trial may admit, there is a "may" here, so it has discretion here and it can use its discretion, and the Appeals Chamber has nothing to do about this. So you're talking about the Appeals Chamber, but the Trial Chamber may with -- at its discretion do what it wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add that 92 ter does not involve a viva voce witness for which there's an examination-in-chief. The only thing you can do with Rule 92 ter is ask questions just to explain some details. So it is a completely different situation than the one we have here. Therefore, I don't believe that Rule 92 ter could be applied here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, please resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is it the Chamber's ruling that I may not ask the foundational questions of the witness regarding his attestation of this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may ask questions on the statement in order to refresh his memory. Yesterday for three hours you asked a number of questions, and according to the answers given you noted that there were some changes maybe in the answer given in relation to what had been signed in the statement at the time. So there on these matters you may ask new questions with this statement, but only to refresh the memory of the witness. However, if you would like to deal with topics that are in the written statement, for example, with the Skorpions without showing the written statement, you can do this, of course, that's an in-chief, that's an examination-in-chief per se.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would note that it's our submission that the scope of examination allowed when a witness statement is admitted under Rule 92 ter allows a witness to also testify in viva voce and that that rule has been applied in that manner in this Tribunal with some variations and consistencies, and I understand that's a point of disagreement by the Bench and you've ruled that I should not attempt to qualify the statement for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think this is what we have said, and I think we stand united in the Presiding Judge's observations. This is -- the question that you have raised is the question of the admission of the statement as such. As far as questions relating to the foundation, if there are any inconsistencies between what the witness has previously stated in his statement and what he testified yesterday, then you may clarify these questions, but other than that, admission of the statement as such is out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I understand that. I want to make sure that if that decision is overturned that I am not left in the position of having failed to demonstrate the foundational requirements for admission so that at a later point in time the statement can be considered as evidence in the case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Appeals Chamber eventually said you were right - it may happen, who knows - then you could always ask the witness to come back and ask him questions on the foundation if you're granted -- your motion is granted by the Appeals Chamber. But all three Judges explained their opinion and they are all -- they're all agreeing. This written statement cannot be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I understand that and I'm not presently seeking its admission. I'm simply trying to lay the foundation so that I can satisfy the requirements if that request is made at the conclusion of his testimony, for instance, because I fear that the effect of the ruling limiting the amount of time that I have to examine the witness will preclude me from going through all of the documents that he has commented on and which are attached to this statement to allow the admission of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't really want to give you any advice, but it is true that I was a Prosecutor at one point in my life, but technically things are very simple. If you want to deal with a specific topic, ask him a question on this topic. Say, Sir, you were here at this moment, what happened, tell us? And then you have your answer. And then you show your document and say, Well, I'm going to show you a document and so forth and so on. This is the way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We have the document on the screen presently and we're -- this is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, can you identify the document on the screen, it's Exhibit 07044?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the first page of something here that is supposed to be my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking on that, do you see your initials at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And let me ask you to turn -- the registrar to turn to page number -- it's the ERN 06031374, and I'll give you the e-court number in a minute, page 39 in e-court in the B/C/S version. It's page 34 in the English version. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you review the document before signing it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You don't recall whether you reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I don't recall. I'm saying that since I signed it, it was probably read out to me or I read it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you look through and indicate whether your initials appear on the bottom of every page? I'll give you the paper copy to allow you to review that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge. Judges, Ms. Christine Dahl is not following your instructions at all. It seems that she wants to cross-examine the witness now. She is not entitled to cross-examine the witness. If I understood your instructions correctly, she is supposed to put questions; and if she's not satisfied with the answer, then perhaps she can remind the witness that he had also said something else or that he had said something different. What she is doing now is cross-examining the witness. Who knows what kind of a state the witness was in when he signed this piece of paper? His signature on this paper doesn't mean a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your objection is overruled, Mr. Seselj. We have a list of documents, exhibits, starting with number 733, which is a video which was shown to the witness. And in the last column regarding this video I say, I recognise volunteer, person I cannot name, don't remember the name. So there are documents that he has seen and recognised, and on the right-hand side -- right-hand column we have the position of the witness regarding a number of documents. For example, for this video 733 he says, I recognised the Chetnik flag without precluding the -- Mrs. Dahl is just asking the witness whether he has recognised the documents. You can continue, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me return to my question and ask Mr. Stoparic to please look at the document and confirm that his initials appear at the bottom of each page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recognise my initials. I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to the chart that's below your signature line that lists videos, photographs, and then followed by exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It's at page 40 in e-court, page 35 in English. I would note, for the record, that this table was created with exhibit numbers applied before the Pre-Trial Judge required a re-numbering of the 65 ter exhibits. I've prepared in the Court binder a table that includes the old number and the new number to assist. I didn't consider I should change the original document, but I did create a sheet for you to see which is which, and I can reproduce the chart for you if you want to use it with the new exhibit numbers separately. That is included as the witness statement in the annex to our consolidated motion. It includes the reference key for the different exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In preparing the table of exhibits, were you shown these documents, including the videos and the photographs listed in the chart?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are the comments on the far right-hand column your comments about the documents, videos, and photographs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really take up that much time now. I can't read each and every one of these comments before I have a look through the entire document, but these should be my comments in relation to the documents that the investigators showed me. Most of the documents are documents that I then saw for the first time in my life. Yes, well, it should be my comments. I can't really read all of them now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is there anything that you're looking at now that makes you think that something was put in there that wasn't your comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, there are many documents. You could select out of them some that could be submitted to the witness and you could ask questions on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That's what I'm turning to, Your Honour. I just wanted to make sure that there wasn't an insinuation that we had somehow put a comment that we ascribed to him that he didn't actually make. And in answering my question the witness said "probably." So I want him to confirm that he's had an opportunity to look at this chart and that it accurately reflects the comments that he made about the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I have an objection. An examination-in-chief cannot be carried out in this way. First of all, the Prosecutor has to show the witness each and every one of these documents in the courtroom once again and then we have to hear his comments. Then if the witness gives a comment that is different from the one he had given previously, then the Prosecutor can jog his memory rather than say en bloc there are many pages here, is this yours, how can he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what the Prosecutor is going to do. She's going to submit documents. So wait for her to do her job. She's going to submit documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So can I ask the witness to answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So before the documents are you submitted to you, Witness, you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, the question was whether what we see here are my comments in relation to certain documents, and I said I assume that that is the case because I cannot read each and every one of them individually now, it would take up a lot of time. I have no reason to doubt that these are my comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to turn to 65 ter Exhibit Number 00657. It should be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your binder which tab is it under or under -- what is the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It's at tab 9, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this document is, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to read it on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can I ask the registrar to zoom out a little bit so the witness can see the entire document including the seal and the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I believe you have this document in the binder. Mr. Usher's going to help you, because this document we see on our screens is also in the binder. So it is tab 9, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's much better this way. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is the document? Let me start by -- who signed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And to whom is the document addressed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is the request being -- the direction being given by the author of the document to the commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that all the volunteers sent by the Serbian Radical Party are being put under your command, that is the commander to whom the letter is addressed or the document, the commander of the volunteers is Slobodan Katic from Belgrade, who is an experienced fighter. He has been appointed their leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is that the same Slobodan Katic that you mentioned in your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only one Slobodan Katic, yes, that's him.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what is the agency or the organization that sent the letter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter was sent by the War Staff of the Serb Radical Party, and the signatory is the chief of the War Staff, Ljubisa Petkovic. There's also a note here which says: "The letter should be read out loud in front of all the fighters."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is there a seal on the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the seal of the Serb Radical Party, or rather, the Main Staff of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you wish me to move the documents into evidence as we proceed or do you want me to wait until the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Yes, you can, but I have a question of the witness because this is a very crucial document which is part of your pre-trial brief as being one exhibit in support of your case. Therefore, this is worthy of a very thorough examination. I have, therefore, very specific questions for the witness on this document. As you said, it is addressed to the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment. The title is very clear because it says: "Commander." In this document it is explained that Mr. Katic is an experienced soldier from Belgrade is appointed commander of volunteers in -- of the volunteers in Vukovar. I'm going to put a very specific and technical question. This commander of the volunteers, in your view, is he the commander of the group of volunteers from Vukovar? Is he going to be the commander or is he going to be the commander of the unit, of the Leva Supoderica unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, you're referring to the new commander, the experienced fighter Slobodan Katic, who is being nominated as the commander, he's being proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is suggested that he should be the new commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment. Is that the way you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter is addressed to the current commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment and the recommendation is that a man is being sent who is to be appointed commander of the volunteers in the Vukovar TO. It doesn't have to mean that he should be the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment. There were other volunteers within the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You already gave an answer to my question. He is going to be appointed commander of the volunteers of the Vukovar TO. Second technical question: In the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I have an objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. There can be no objection when a question is put by a Judge, that's the first thing. Secondly, as part of the cross-examination you'll have the opportunity to come back to this issue. The witness has just told us that Slobodan Katic, in his view - he may be wrong but that's what he says - is hereby being appointed of the -- as commander of the volunteers of the TO in Vukovar. If you don't agree with this, when you cross-examine him you can raise questions on this. Second question I want to put. I see the second paragraph that Mr. Vakic from Nis is going to be appointed the commander of the volunteers from Nis. Is this the way things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here, Your Honour, that he will be appointed platoon commander or platoon leader of the volunteers from Nis, so he's not going to be the detachment commander but, rather, a platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fourth paragraph, this is of particular interest to me. Indeed this War Staff of the Serbian Radical Party states that the commander of this unit is to issue to all volunteers a certificate, and everything is described. We should have the date the person enters the unit, et cetera. This procedure as described in the fourth paragraph, was it applied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the normal procedure. Without this certificate, a participant in the war operations cannot prove that he was a participant. He needs it if he's wounded, he needs it to get his salary or to prove that he's a war invalid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, do you have a mention of this certificate in the military booklet - we saw an example of that through yours - or is it to be found in another document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has the same purpose. The military booklet has only four columns and they were not sufficient. The certificate had the same significance as the stamp in the war booklet in war. It's proof that a certain person spent a certain period of time in that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain to me why in your military booklet we see nothing about Vukovar in your case? Because you were in Vukovar, you may have participated in combat action. How is it that there is no mention of it in your military booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I received a certificate issued to me by a major, and his name eludes me at the moment, in Velepromet with the approval of the commander of Leva Supoderica saying that from such and such a date to such and such date I was a member of Leva Supoderica within the 1st Guards Brigade. At one point the technical service of the 1st Guards Brigade brought salaries to Vukovar and distributed them to the fighters, but many of us were on leave at that time. So when the salaries were distributed they didn't leave the rest of the money there, they sent it back to Belgrade. On one occasion about a month and a half after that I happened to be in Belgrade, so I dropped in in the barracks in Topcider. I went to the command of the guards brigade. I asked for Captain Radic and Zirojevic. Zirojevic was there, he took me to an officer who was in charge of these technical matters, and he issued to me the salary that I earned in Vukovar, but I had to leave that certificate with him as proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... ask questions before I give the floor back to Ms. Dahl. In this document it can be seen that the commander of the Nis section has been suggested as -- was suggested to the commander of the detachment to be appointed as a commander of the Nis platoon. As far as you are concerned, was there a similar document made out for you asking for the -- or asking of the detachment commander for you to be appointed a platoon leader? It may be so, it may not be, I don't know. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I think I explained how I became a platoon commander. On my arrival in Vukovar and joining the Leva Supoderica Detachment I was already a squad leader or squad commander. After the first action we had in Vukovar when my platoon commander disappeared in that action, he went missing, I assume he was captured and killed. He was a lieutenant. And then at the proposal of my fellow soldiers in the platoon, I was appointed platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... very last question which will encapsulate the whole issue, the whole problem. In this Leva Supoderica Detachment there were various platoons, you were heading one of them. With regard to the volunteers, as far as you know, were all platoon commanders appointed upon this being proposed by the SRS War Staff or were there situations such as yours, for instance, in which a platoon commander would be appointed by other -- by the other soldiers? Because, for instance, a sergeant disappeared, which was your case, without any intervention by the SRS, by the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my personal opinion is, and I'm most convinced, that the War Staff and the Serb Radical Party did not concern itself with who would be a squad or a platoon leader. They could nominate a commander, but it was his problem how he would organize his unit, what people he would replace, dismiss, or promote, and this is a proposal. Probably this man had certain merits and he was being proposed, but it was not the usual practice for a squad or platoon leader to be nominated by the War Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... in this time, Ms. Dahl, but this document which is part -- or is mentioned in your pre-trial brief really deserved being looked into.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I tender the document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the admission, the registrar is first going to give a number for the booklet, yesterday's booklet, and then we'll have a number for this document. And if this way of going about it turns out to be too complicated, we'll do it otherwise. Two numbers, first for the military booklet and then for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I have an objection. I think that not a single document can be entered into the file and admitted into evidence until the examination is over because the witness has now only expressed his opinion on the contents of the document but he has not confirmed its authenticity or told you that he has ever seen it, so I think Your Honours have to wait for the cross-examination in order to see whether the document may be admitted into evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has now decided a number will be given if after the cross-examination or during it you think that there is no probative value, that it is a forged document, you may ask for the document to be removed, but it's going to be given a number for the time being. And you're right, you will cross-examine, and if you think that this document should not be admitted you can say so then. But provisionally speaking, since this document has been submitted to the witness, it can be given a number. So two numbers for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The 65 ter number, number 32, that's the military booklet, will be MFI P22 and the current document will be MFI P23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was Slobodan Katic a Chetnik commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might say that he was, yes. Well, a Chetnik commander, a commander of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask that we turn next to tab 16 in the Court binder, 65 ter number 00764. I'll ask that the registrar give the witness a paper copy for ease of reference. With reference to 65 ter number 764, can you determine from the face of the document who issued it or which agency -- I'm sorry, which agency issued it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here it was issued by the Serbian Radical Party and signed by the chief Ljubisa Petkovic. I believe he was the chief of the War Staff or Crisis Staff, whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is there a seal from the Serbian Radical Party on the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of December, 1991. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this is a -- what this list is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it's a list of men, volunteers, with their date of birth, place of birth, occupation, from when they were engaged in the Territorial Defence, and what duty they performed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you recognise whether or not it is a list of War Staff members? Take a look at the names of the individuals who are listed. And I'd like to ask you to answer that based on your knowledge of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Petkovic, son of Dusan, he was in the War Staff, but, Madam Prosecutor, I have tell you that I don't know who the members of the War Staff were. I don't know what their names were. I know about Ljubisa Petkovic and Zoran Drazilovic. As for the others, they may have been added on or replaced but I couldn't tell you. I can't look at this list and say, Yes, these are the members of the War Staff of the Serb Radical Party except for Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Will you familiar with documents issued by the Radical Party's War Staff during the war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions I did see something, some documents in Kameni's staff, but they were either -- they referred either to prizes to be given or to proposals of some sort. I never felt that the War Staff was duty-bound to issue orders ordering war actions. I don't think they had the right to do that. I don't think they could do that, propose to us how we should behave. They might, for example, collect some help we needed, cigarettes, underwear, and such-like, things we couldn't get on time from the JNA. I saw some trivial documents of that kind, but I don't remember them in detail. Madam Prosecutor, I never entered into any kind of conflict with my commander and I never dabbled in matters that were none of my business, so I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What kinds of activities did the War Staff organize with respect to volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that they organized gathering volunteers and sending them on to a JNA unit. If we're talking about 1991 and Vukovar, then to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem under the command of a JNA unit or brigade which was there on that terrain. Many people from Republika Srpska, and later on from Croatia or the Krajina, applied. Local commanders could do that. I saw some of your documents which show this, so they could organize us, send us out into the war theatre, and while we were there they could send us assistance. They could also give us legal assistance if we were wounded, if we had any problems in claiming our rights from a hospital or somewhere, they could help us to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while listening to you I have a problem with this document, and I'm going to ask you about it. Your answer's important. There's a list of people, you only know two of them, Petkovic and Drazilovic, fine. But while looking at this list of people, I note that this is a list that seems to come from the Serbian Radical Party. Now, when I see the qualifications of people, I see that Mr. Petkovic has been part of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia since October 25, 1991, and then in brackets it says "(Chief of War Staff)." Very well. It's the same for all the others, they all belong to the Western Slavonia Territorial Defence. This is what is written on this document. Here's my question: According to you, is this a list of people who are part of the War Staff of the Serb Radical Party that have positions within this party or is it a list of people who are part of the Western Slavonia Territorial Defence who may also be member of the Serb Radical Party, with the specific point being that the number one seemed to be the Chief of the War Staff and also is from the Radical Party. So how do you interpret this document exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says quite clearly in this document all the details there, first name, last name, father's name, date and place of birth, civilian occupation, and then it says: "In the Territorial Defence since the 25th of October, 1991," I'm referring to Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic, and then in brackets it says: "(Chief of War Staff)," so what duty he performed in the War Staff, but for each one it says here when they joined the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia or it says here just Slavonia. So they may have participated in the Territorial Defence but it says here only when they joined and it doesn't say until when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we need an MFI document -- MFI number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like to turn to what's in the court binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please repeat the number because it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, MFI P24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, for your information, number MFI P24 is a provisional number. After the cross-examination this number may become final, depending on what will be said and depending on the Trial Chamber's decision. Mrs. Dahl --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, briefly. I'm afraid there might be some confusion. This document mentions Western Slavonia. This witness was in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. These are two territories several hundred kilometres distant from each other. This witness was not in Western Slavonia. I'm just saying this to avoid confusion. You may do what you like about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can look into this during your cross-examination. Mrs. Dahl, please resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would just like to point out that we will have other witnesses who can discuss the content of the document. I'd like to turn next to what is in Court binder at tab number 17, that's 65 ter number 770, and I'll hand the witness a paper copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the tab number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 17. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, can you take a look at the document and tell me what it is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we see a request by the Chetnik commander of Vukovar, Slobodan Katic, from Zemun addressed to the Chief of the War Staff, Ljubisa Petkovic, and he is proposing that certain people be promoted. Reading this list it says: To the commander of -- Milan Lancuzanin, a.k.a., Kameni; Predrag Milojevic, commander of the 1st Assault Platoon; Milosav -- Milovan Tomic - I know this man, he arrived after the fall of Vukovar, but he asked for this promotion - "Vujovic Miroljub," who was not a member of Leva Supoderica, he was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, and it says so here. Then Stanko Vujanovic, chief of TO in Vukovar. In other words, he's proposing that these people be promoted or rewarded in some way. They were not all members, either of the Radical Party or of Leva Supoderica. So in my view it's quite normal for Katic to make this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. The 9th of December, 1991, yes, Vukovar was already in our hands there, it had already fallen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. For the sake of the public, the contents of the document have to be made public. It says here that Katic is asking Ljubisa Petkovic to propose to someone, it doesn't say to whom, but it should be said precisely for the sake of the public. He's asking that Ljubisa Petkovic propose. It's not Katic who's making the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had noticed this. Witness, please, this document bears a stamp coming from the Vukovar municipal Territorial Defence. We agree. This is not a document coming from the Serb Radical Party. Secondly, I notice that Mr. Slobodan Katic seems to be the captain -- seems to be a captain within the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, and he's asking Petkovic and Rankic to promote a number of people. Is this how this document should be interpreted? Unless I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, that's right. Slobodan Katic informs -- or rather, he proposes to Ljubisa Petkovic that Ljubisa Petkovic propose further on at higher instances these particular persons for a promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This seems to mean that all these people, Lancuzanin, Tomic, Milojevic, and so on, are people who belong to the Territorial Defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by the date we can see that Vukovar had already fallen. After the fall of Vukovar the 1st Guards Brigade withdrew from Vukovar and the Leva Supoderica Detachment was disbanded. The manpower who were from Serbia were returned to their homes or perhaps sent further on to other territories for war operations, and he with the rest of this detachment of Leva Supoderica was attached to the Territorial Defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the added value you're providing us is that Vukovar fell -- had fallen at the time and that the situation as it is after December 9, 1991. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: To whom would Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Rankic propose these individuals for promotion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these people were supposed to be promoted in terms of military rank, then probably with the representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army, they would submit a proposal to the representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army. I don't see who else. Who else can give them a military rank? Who else can promote them except the JNA or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What's your understanding of the role or authority of a Chetnik commander in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this was typed out by Mr. Slobodan Katic. He himself calls himself a Chetnik commander and a captain for Vukovar. I doubt that he has a particular document stating that Chetnik commander, captain for Vukovar, and Vukovar is not such a small town to have a captain heading it. He calls himself a Chetnik commander, captain. He considers himself that, but believe me that in terms of official procedures, nobody would have written this that way. He's simply writing it that way because he's sending this letter to Ljubisa Petkovic in the War Staff and, quite simply, this is the way the man writes this. He calls himself a Chetnik commander, captain for the town of Vukovar, which is not to say that that was his position in Vukovar, the Chetnik commander. It's not that he had a document stating something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question after Mrs. Dahl's question. As of -- at that date, who headed the TO of Vukovar, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this date, yes, the 9th of December, 1991, I know of the commander during the war and after the war of the TO -- I mean at least at first during the first two or three months after the fall of Vukovar it was Miroljub Vujanovic -- Vujovic, Miroljub Vujovic. I always confuse him and Stanko Vujanovic. Miroljub was the commander of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So tell us, if Mr. Miroljub Vujovic was commander of the TO, why isn't he is charge of promoting the people who are under his orders? Why does he have to go through Petkovic for that? What presented Mr. Miroljub Vujovic from promoting X, Y, or Z? And something that probably everybody noticed that Mr. Kameni ends up here in the Territorial Defence. Since he is listed here as a person for which a promotion is requested. So can you shed some light on this, please, or isn't it the fact that the Leva Supoderica was just part and parcel of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why commander Kameni is on the list of the Territorial Defence, I explained that a few moments ago. At this point in time we're talking about the 9th of December, 1991. At this time there is no intensive fighting. Vukovar had been liberated. Kameni disbands Leva Supoderica quite literally. People go back to Serbia, people who were volunteers, and for the most part the volunteers were from Serbia. They go home on vacation, even the 1st Guards Brigade withdraws and Leva Supoderica no longer exists as such. They join and he himself is duty-bound to join the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. I don't find anything strange there. There is no longer a war, he is no longer within the 1st Guards Brigade and he is not the commander of Leva Supoderica, he is with the Territorial Defence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the transcript, as of December 9, 1991, following the fall of Vukovar, the Leva Supoderica Detachment was disbanded, people who were part of it go elsewhere, which is why Kameni then ends up in the Vukovar Territorial Defence. This is how you interpret the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This date is not the date when Leva Supoderica was disbanded; that happened before. These people went home before that. Milan Lancuzanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was it disbanded, if you remember, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediately after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Dahl --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. After this disbandment, the TO still existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Combat operations are still taking place, but not in town, outside town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Territorial Defence is under command -- the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the JNA was there, yes, yes, it was under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Commander Katic come from Belgrade with SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at this point in time he voluntarily stays in the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. That is the way it seems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This issue of volunteers, it really is heart of the matter. You did your military service in the JNA, you were an officer, apparently you had some responsibilities, even if it was at a limited level. You are the first witness, there may be others, but since you are the first witness I'm going to raise the question with you. In 1991, back then, the status of people like you, what was it? Was it that they had because of problems connected with the events and the war, did they have to be in the army or could you be a civilian without necessarily being forced to be in the army? Or still were all civilians, say from 18 to 65 years of age, could they all be called up as soldiers? What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civilians from the age of 18 -- no, 19, 20, up to the age of 50 could have been called up by the military or they could have joined a unit voluntarily. However, that is only if they were able-bodied for military service and if they had served their military service while they were young. If a medical commission had declared them incapable of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your view, in 1991 all civilians from 19 to 50 years of age could be called or drafted to serve in the army. However, if they were not called they could be volunteers in order to join the army, provided they met certain conditions. Is this how the situation was back then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Able-bodied military-aged men could have been called up to the reserve force of the JNA or the TO or the reserve police force. Also, they -- if they had not been called up and if they feel they were needed to go out there to take part in the defence, they could have volunteered to go there. That is how it functioned. According to our constitution, that was quite legal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So based on the constitution and individuals aged 40 who had not been called up by the army was free to stay at home, doing his business quietly, but for some unknown reason or his own reason he could think that he would be a volunteer and join the army. Is that so? Is that how the situation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that person could have become a volunteer at any moment; however, there is another thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not that they could become volunteers because that means that the one deciding to volunteer, that carries an intention, a will. I'm asking about from the point of view of the authorities, the military authorities or the political ones. That's the relation between the authority, the political authority and the citizens of the country. In 1991 was it so that the army could tell any given citizen that they should join the army and then not call up the individuals, but the so-called volunteers could of their own accord decide to join the army, so turn to the army to say, I want to fight, I want to be a volunteer. When I say "individuals," I mean men and women alike.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you a very simple explanation now. I see where the problem lies. The army has its own policy of recruitment and its own way of doing things, and they know when they need or do not need smaller or larger groups of reservists. A volunteer could be equal. There is no difference. One always said "volunteers," a volunteer volunteered, whereas a reservist had been called up. That's the only difference. Later on everything was different. When taking in volunteers the organization that takes in this volunteer is duty-bound to look at your military booklet to see the rubric that is called collection point, that is to see whether in your military booklet you have already been designated a reservist, whether you had been designated a reservist but simply had not been called up yet. If you did have a collection point, that is called war assignment, then you were not accepted as a volunteer; however, a person who did not have a war assignment could have joined the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was a very important question, like all the questions I put. You now speak about the reservists. This issue of the reservists, if you have a volunteer does he or she become automatically a reservist? Meaning that they could be called at any time to fight, could be called by the JNA or by the TO? So there it is. Can you answer this question. And then if I understand you properly if, for instance, this volunteer is a supporter of the Serbian Radical Party, the SRS is going to check that that person has the status of a reservist in order to trigger his assignment to a unit. Is that how the system worked because this would have had a whole host of consequences. So we has Judges must be very clear on this. Can you make that more specific to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav People's Army at any point in time could carry out a mobilisation and get a certain number of reservists for themselves that they would later on send out to various assignments. People who had not been called up to join the reserve force at that point in time and are able-bodied and are military conscripts, they can have war assignments designated in their military booklets. They should not volunteer because it is possible that they would be called up at some point in time as reservists, so people who organized volunteers and sent them likewise to the JNA always had a look at this. They checked whether you as an individual had a war assignment; if you did, they could not send you to the volunteer unit. Regardless of whether it's a volunteer unit or not, it has identical rights and responsibilities like reservists. If you look at military -- if you look at my military booklet, you will see what my wartime assignment is. That is how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that Ms. Dahl listened to you carefully because what you said seems to me absolutely essential. Please proceed, Ms. Dahl. I was bound to address these issues because they are at the very heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I welcome the questions from the Bench to satisfy information needs that you might have, so I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Could you discuss your decision to volunteer with the radicals and how that came about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I became a member of the Leva Supoderica Detachment I was not sent from Belgrade like some of the members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment that had already been established by then. At first I registered as a volunteer with the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Zapadni Srem, I took part in combat operations for two weeks, and then I joined Leva Supoderica. I went to Belgrade, in Belgrade Ljubisa Petkovic sent us to Bubanj Potok. In Bubanj Potok we were trained, we were equipped, we had drills, we had target practice, and then we were sent to the place where we would be engaged in combat operations. If I understand you correctly, you asked me what led me to do something like this. You see, I took part in the fighting in Vukovar with the members of the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. Although I'm a witness here and although I mentioned the names of individuals who engaged in deviant behaviour, those names cannot be added to the names of honourable Serb soldiers. However, I have to tell you that an enormous number of people were honourable, brave, courageous soldiers. And as we say in Serbia, among wheat there is -- there are always some grains that are not good. I mean, there can be some crazy men who did do some things somewhere, but I cannot say that the Leva Supoderica Detachment did this in an organized and constant fashion. These were individual cases that led to these atrocious crimes. Also, these crimes were committed on the other side. The Croats were no less -- well, all of it was the same. So I trusted the people I fought with. I trusted Mr. Seselj in the Serb Radical Party. I liked the programme. I liked their presentation. I liked the programme, and I believed, like the Serb Radical Party programme believed, that we should defend our interests and everything; that's why I joined.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was in control of Bubanj Potok and provided the training you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bubanj Potok was always under the control of the JNA. Later on the Army of Yugoslavia, now the Army of Serbia. This was a military facility, it was under the control of a brigade commander who was in charge of that facility or I don't know who. As for training and equipment, it was the JNA officers who trained and equipped us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Before you volunteered with the Territorial Defence, you attended the rally by Dr. Seselj in Sid; am I understanding correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I attended this rally at a football stadium, but I also said that I don't know whether it was beforehand or afterwards. It was a long time ago. Now, was it before I had already taken part in the war or after I had taken part in the war, I really -- well, I think I've told you many times that I have a problem with dates and, quite simply, I do not remember them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to look at paragraph 55 of your 2006 statement so that you can refresh your recollection. It's at -- I'll pass you the paper copy for your convenience. It's 65 ter number 7044, paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection about when you attended the rally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that it was the summer of 1991. That is to say that that's what I said then, but I still cannot assert that that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you recall the speech that Mr. Seselj made?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time Mr. Seselj made a speech -- it was always the same one, regardless of whether it was held in Sid or in Krusevac. At that moment it was based on the social-political situation that we had, that there was an imminent threat of war, the war had already started or had already started, and then the HDZ, the Croatian democratic community -- well, during those several months it was identical, regardless of where it was held. We've already discussed this paragraph. We've talked about it with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Seselj advocate a solution for the residents of Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense? That they should leave Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was he making suggestions about expelling Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment he did use some similar terms, but at that moment he had to -- well, didn't have to, but he said that and there was an enormous number of refugees in Serbia by then. I cannot quote Mr. Seselj. Later on he did advocate some principles of retortion, but I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently you are somebody who listened to Dr. Seselj's speech. We'll see other videos, but that's not the issue right now. You were there during the summer of 1991 in this village of Kukujevci, sorry if I don't pronounce properly. Could you tell the Judges whether based on your memory -- what was the tenor, the contents of the speech? What did he say precisely? What is your recollection of what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you've just said that it was the village of Kukujevci in the summer of 1991. He was not in the village of Kukujevci in the summer of 1991, he was there much later. He visited the village of Kukujevci I think that when the war in Croatia was already over or there was some kind of stagnation at a particular level but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... did you hear a speech by Mr. Seselj? Say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I'm trying to tell you, that I heard about this in Kukujevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was it exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it a speech made as part of a political campaign or as part of another setting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly it might have been within presidential elections or something else. Quite simply, the village of Kukujevci was in -- was of interest because there had been an exchange carried out. People who lived in Kukujevci had exchanged their houses or apartments with Serbs from Croatia. That was a good example of Croatians -- Croats having exchanged their houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and tell us -- well, 1991, I would not be able to recall anything that was said by somebody in 1991, but maybe your memory's better than mine. Try to tell us what struck you in Mr. Seselj's speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say - I can't quote him - but I can say how I felt after hearing Mr. Seselj's speech and what I thought. That's how I can best describe what he said. As a listener, he warned me of the danger of the resurrected Ustasha - I'm using my own words now, Your Honour - who had risen like vampires from the grave. He spoke of the threat of a new genocide. He said we were under threat, that there were actual situations which had already led to murders and expulsions. Listening to Mr. Seselj I concluded that that was actually the situation, and as a man, a Serb and a citizen, I had to play an active role. I would have to participate sooner or later. I didn't think it would be the very next day. And let me stress that it was not Mr. Seselj's speech alone that prompted me to become a volunteer. Quite simply, listening to his speeches at the time, I came to understand certain matters in my own way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl -- Ms. Dahl, I'm being told -- time flies. Unfortunately, time does pass and we are under some time constraints. We're going to have a break, it will be a 30-minute break so that Mr. Seselj can check the fax machine. We shall resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed, somewhat belatedly because Mr. Seselj was expecting a fax. Mr. Seselj, tell your associates to send faxes early in the morning to avoid this kind of situation where you have to wait for the fax machine to give you copies during breaks, especially if you're expecting 80 or 100 pages. So please instruct your associates so that they take into account the fact that we have breaks that last at most 20 minutes or within 20 minutes you have to go to the fax machine and look at documents. Do your best. We will resume. In theory we finish by 12.30, so you should finish by 12.30, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender Exhibit 770, that 65 ter was the last document we were discussing regarding the request from the Territorial Defence for promotion of Chetnik commanders.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI P25.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, before the break we were discussing the speech at Kukujevci and also the speech in Sid, and I want to turn your attention to the speech in Sid. Did that speech -- can you describe the manner in which Mr. Seselj gave the speech, his manner of speaking?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the first time I heard Mr. Seselj speak was at the Radnicki Football Club in Sid, I think almost all the citizens of Sid were there, and the manner in which Seselj spoke -- I'm not sure I understand your question properly. We all know how Seselj interprets speeches. You want me now to describe this?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes. Was he loud or soft? Passionate? Withdrawn? I'd like you to describe the manner in which Mr. Seselj gave his speech.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj speaks loud, he is passionate in his speeches. You yourself have had the chance to see how Mr. Seselj speaks. You can't expect me to find the words to describe this. Quite simply, as a listener you find him interesting. He's an interesting speaker. He knows how to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: From your observations of the people there and the volunteers you later served with, did Mr. Seselj's speech influence people's decision to go volunteer at the war front?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether he affected the decision a hundred per cent, I don't know, but they could find inspiration or -- well, not inspiration but how can we say that? In Serbia our eyes were opened, quite simply. Everyone had their own version and everybody experienced it in his or her way so that the speeches were of a nationalist nature and that was fashionable at the time in our political life, it wasn't only Seselj who spoke like that, so that we as listeners and citizens liked hearing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was he urging people to volunteer for the Yugoslav Army, directly to them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quote Mr. Seselj. I can't say whether he said, I invite you all right now after this conversation to go to the Territorial Defence and apply and volunteer. I can't say that, but he explained the historical situation, he explained the kind of dangers facing us. So if you were the least bit patriotic, you would conclude that it was your duty to take part. Some were fit to take up weapons, others to take up a pencil, but quite simply I personally found that he awoke in me my nationalist consciousness, not only he, I repeat, but Mr. Seselj and his speeches played a good part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that it woke your nationalist consciousness. Could you tell me what nationalist consciousness is in your book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before that, while I was a pupil in primary and secondary school, we learned parts of history in the way it was written according to me the winners of World War II. And in our case it was the Partizans or the national liberation movement under the leadership of the Communist Party and Josip Broz Tito, so that in everything we studied, not only citizens of Serbia but all the citizens of the former Yugoslavia, we did not learn a lot about nationalism in our own histories. We did learn a definition of nationalism provided by the communists. Nationalism was a taboo subject. In 1991 or as early as 1990 people spoke up who presented history in a different way, and I saw this as having a realistic foundation. Because in the history I learned at school the Chetniks and the Ustasha were treated in an identical way. They were seen as identical, as enemies, both sides, but we know that the Ustasha were given their own state, they had concentration camps, and so on, whereas the Chetniks had none of that in World War II. So that identifying those two movements as identical was not in my view realistic. And in 1990/1991, a number of people turned up who told us that this was not the case. I as an individual, I can't speak for others, I thought that this was realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to the speech in Kukujevci that you attended. What was, to your recollection, the core of that speech?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me now to recall on what occasion he spoke, whether it was an election campaign or just a visit. The venue was chosen, Kukujevci, that is, because as I said, the majority of the Croatian population that had lived in Kukujevci before that time had exchanged their houses with the Serbs from Croatia. At the point in time when Mr. Seselj visited that village and gave his speech, there were many new villagers and he addressed them. As far as I can recall, he spoke on topics that these people were interested in. They had changed states, they had changed houses, the war was still going on, I think. I've told you many times, Madam Prosecutor, that I'm not good at dates. I don't have a good head for dates so I don't even try to remember them, so I can't really pin-point the time, but it wasn't 1991 or 1992. It may have been 1993. It was when people had already exchanged houses and arrived there and the topic of his speech was in line with that. I can't remember literally what he said. I found all of Seselj's speeches at the time interesting. They all had a beginning and an end and a story that explained things to us. I simply think that the topic of that speech was concerned with the issues that the Serbs who had exchanged their houses with Croats were interested in. But I can't say that with certainty because it was so long ago. At that time I participated in that, I assisted with providing security in front of the Municipal Staff of the Radical Party in Sid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. This village of Kukujevci, was it a village which was before, during, or after the war also inhabited by Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The majority of the population had been Croat, I think more than 90 per cent before the war, before 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Mr. Seselj's speech, did he make any reference to the need for the Croats to leave the village, for them to leave Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj at that time in this village addressed the majority Serbian population which had in the meantime exchanged their homes and their houses with the Croats. The Croats had already left the village of Kukujevci, exchanged their houses with those of Serbs, and gone to Croatia. So at the time he spoke, he was addressing the Serb majority because the Croats were no longer present in those numbers. Whether he spoke about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've said this already in answering one of the Prosecutor's questions. Now I'd like you to answer my own question. Did he speak to the fact that Croats should have left -- I mean the Croats who were still there, that they should have left, abandoned the village and as -- generally that the Croats should leave Serbia, the territory, the Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj in some of his addresses was in the habit of saying that certain Croats were duty-bound to leave Serbia. He was referring to Croats who had participated in the war. It was not impossible for a Croat already living in Serbia not to have left through certain channels to Croatia and join the ZNG and participate in the war as a ZNG member. When he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, during this specific speech, I'm not talking about speeches in general, in this speech did he make any reference to that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. Maybe he didn't because the exchange had already taken place in that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, what you stated in the witness statement was an incomplete or erroneous memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying it's impossible that Mr. Seselj in his address to the people mentioned the need for exchanges of houses, for Croats to move to Croatia and Serbs to come there, but I cannot assert with certainty that it was at that time in Kukujevci that he said that in that way. Quite simply, I do remember such statements made by him, but now I cannot say that he said that at that particular point in time because it's confused in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned exchanges of houses. Could you be more specific. Did Serbs and Croats agree with a view to exchanging houses? For instance, did Serbs buy Croat houses for Croats to go back to Croatia or was there a forced exchange in which it was made clear to the Croats that they had to leave the village so that the Serbs then in Croatia could come to the village? There are many possibilities. You seem to have been in this village since you were in charge of taking care of the security during the speech in the village. So what can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time when the trial started and when the Croats in -- or rather, the procedure, the process started, when the Croats in Kukujevci expressed a desire to go to Croatia an agency called Lasta was opened, first in Kukujevci and then in Sid which dealt with these matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... extremely important. You are saying that at the time when this issue was addressed there was an agency that settled in the village. Was it a real estate agency or was it a government agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The owner of the agency was a Serb who had come from Croatia. He was probably a lawyer by occupation. He opened an agency called Lasta, one in the village of Kukujevci, one in the village of Sid. Through that agency many carried out exchanges. As for forcible exchanges, something that might appear to be forcible exchanges happened later on when Krajina fell under the pressure of the Croatian -- the so-called Croatian military Operation Storm and a vast number of refugees from that area passed through the village of Kukujevci and they were sent on to Western Srem, Slavonia, and Baranja, and they passed through that village. Some of them entered Croat houses. At that point the Croats moved out and went to Croatia, and later on they agreed with the people who had moved into their houses and they legalised the exchange. That was the only thing I remember that might resemble something done by force because a huge group of refugees arrived in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listening to you, prior to Dr. Seselj's speech there was an agency that set up in Kukujevci and there's also one in Sid. Sid is in Croatia or where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sid is in Serbia and the village of Kukujevci is in the Sid municipality. It's a local commune which was part of the Sid municipality. Those two agencies were owned by one and the same man, but they were in two locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me respond, the Lasta agency was opened before Mr. Seselj gave his speech in Kukujevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this agency has two offices, one in Sid, the other in Kukujevci. It is then going to settle the issue of apartments by offering to Croats to leave their houses, but then Croats leaving their houses, are they going to sell them? What are the offices going to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the agency knocked on people's doors, going house to house, whether they did it in some other way, I can't tell you. To me it seems reasonable to assume that the Croats wanted to leave and that they welcomed the agency. The agency established contacts and searched for appropriate houses of approximately equal value so that they could be exchanged, a house from the village of Kukujevci with a house somewhere in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So either people would sell or houses would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... there was an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this was known to everybody?
