utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to return to your testimony where you said you couldn't remember the content of Mr. Seselj's speech in Kukujevci. Can you please look at your statement and read to yourself paragraphs 60, 61, and 62. This is 65 ter number 7044.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does reviewing your statement refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Dahl, I don't want to sound like someone who has learned something off by heart. I didn't read this before the hearing to jog my memory, so I'm trying to ask -- I'm trying to answer your questions now to the best of my recollection as I remember them now. I can't use the same words when describing an event at different points in time. I'm trying to give you the main gist of what happened. Everything I've read here agrees with what I've just said answering your questions and the questions of the Trial Chamber. Quite simply, there are more details in the statement. Mr. Seselj's rhetoric was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that the core concept of his rhetoric was expulsion of ethnic Croats and the achievement of a concept of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leading question, Mrs. Dahl. This is a leading question, Mrs. Dahl. Could you please reformulate, rephrase your question. Asking him what Mr. Seselj said.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the core concept behind Mr. Seselj's speeches that you heard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj spoke -- you probably are referring to the concept of a Greater Serbia. He even determined the borders which, according to his research, were the Serbian ethnic borders. I know, Madam Prosecutor, how it affected me. I cannot know how it affected a Croat listening to Mr. Seselj's speech. I believe that a Croat might have been frightened by the speech. I can't know what was in the heads of people who were not Serbs and who heard Mr. Seselj's speeches. That may have been your question, I'm not sure. The concept of a Greater Serbia is something that's in the party platform of the Serbian Radical Party, and many people in Serbia are aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what are the political borders that Mr. Seselj was advocating?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not political borders, they're state borders, territorial borders. Maybe it was interpreted as political borders. It was Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, parts of Dalmatia, Lika, Banja, Kordun, Western Srem. He explained this by mentioning the Karlobag-Karlovac-Ogulin-Virovitica line. I am not sure I remember it correctly, but that was the ethnic territory Dr. Seselj believed belonged to us Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And where does the Karlobag-Karlovac-Ogulin-Virovitica line go through?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the towns you listed are in Croatia from the Primorje region. So Dalmatia is in there -- well, look at it on the map. I can't really say that off the top of my head in geographical terms, but all of these towns are in the present Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you 65 ter number 7008. I'm going to pass it -- it's in the map book, the court binder at map 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If I can ask the registrar to give the witness the paper copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it in your binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was in the map binder, so we'll put it up on the ELMO so you can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Place it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is question? [Interpretation] What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you look at this and say whether, with your understanding of what Mr. Seselj was advocating, if this shaded area represents the Greater Serbia border?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you indicate for the Judges where the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica, that would be that line, that would be the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And you referred to a man who opened a real estate agency called Lasta. Was he associated with the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Radical Party in Sid and, to start with, he was only a sponsor because he earned a certain amount of money through his agency, through his work as an agent. He earned a percentage. So he sponsored the Municipal Staff in Sid to start with. The Municipal Staff had certain expenses and he was one of their sponsors. Later on he was a member of the Serb Radical Party in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And is it your understanding that he had a financial interest in persuading people to leave and exchange their houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said a few moments ago that I don't know whether he went from one house to another and contacted people or whether people contacted him asking for his assistance. It's a privately owned agency so he did have a personal interest because that's the way he earned money.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, referring to the Kukujevci speech, was Mr. Seselj advocating the cleansing or expulsion of Croats from the entire area of Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether he said that, whether he put it that way, in the village of Kukujevci is something I cannot tell now. I can only assume that he did present one of his thesis that Croats should leave Serbia, live in their own land of Croatia because it was clear to all by then that there could be no more life together. Now, I cannot say that he said it at 10.15 at the square in the village of Kukujevci. I don't know, really. And once more, may I highlight that at the time when Mr. Seselj made his speech in the village of Kukujevci I was authorised by the Radical Party of Sid to help because this was a legal gathering. It was registered with the Ministry of the Interior, but we helped them with providing security. So as for part of my stay at this rally, I was quite busy with that task of mine, to help with the security there. So it's not that I always paid attention to what Mr. Seselj was saying in his speech and perhaps that's why I don't remember some things and on the other hand it's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that Mr. Seselj has approved of the departure of Croats from that town?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he approved that because he publicly advocated the principle of retortion and he asked the authorities in Serbia to do that. He agreed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by -- when you're using the word "the principle of retortion"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's simple. It is well-known that an enormous number of Serbs were expelled from the territory of Croatia to Serbia. An enormous number of Serbs from areas of Croatia where there had never been any combat operations had left. There can be a village, say, like Kukujevci, there are no combat operations, but say Serbs lived in that kind of village in Croatia and then we were supposed to respond in the same way. Perhaps I don't understand it right, but that is the way I understand retortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With respect to what you know about Croats who left the area, did they leave because they felt their lives were in danger?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had that feeling, yes. Nothing surprising. They had that feeling. We are two peoples at war already, and this war was assuming a religious proportion too, the Orthodox against the Catholics, and the Serbs living in Zagreb had the same feeling. Perhaps it seems strange to you, but it's quite a normal phenomenon to me in that kind of environment, that somebody fears for his or her life and wants to go to a state that he considers to be his mainstream state, the Croats to Croatia, the Serbs to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you aware of Croat persons who were swindled in the process of exchanging their homes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion a Croat from my street moved to Croatia in that way and another man came to his house. Later on when the situation calmed down, when people from Croatian started coming to Serbia again and vice versa, he came to see his old neighbours and he said that he was dissatisfied with that exchange. Also, many Serbs in Kukujevci, Gibarac and Sot said that they were also dissatisfied with what they had left and what they got here. So there were such feelings on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are mentioning this example of a neighbour. Well, my attention was drawn by the fact that you just said he was dissatisfied with that exchange. So my conclusion is that this Croat left for Croatia, obtained an apartment over there, but finally felt like he'd been -- well, he was very dissatisfied with that exchange in the end. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In that way he spoke to us as his old neighbours that he was dissatisfied in terms of financial resources and probably he meant his overall situation in Croatia. I did not put any more in-depth questions to him. I just listened to him for a few moments and I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But do you know how all this occurred? When he left for Croatia, it's the Croats who gave him an apartment or is it with the money he obtained when he left his house, his villa, that he was able to buy a house or was everything organized by the agency, which means that it's the agency that would have found a house in Croatia and that told him, Go there and a Serb living in Croatia will take your place here. Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It worked only in one way. Only the owner of the house -- of a house of a Serb from Croatia could enter the house of a Croat from Serbia who wanted to exchange houses with him. Now, whether they would add some extra money, that depended on each and every individual contact contract. I don't know. The Lasta agency had its office in Sid, in Vukovar, in Vinkovci, that's how they worked, and they got certain percentages depending on their estimate of the value of the real estate involved. So a Serb from Croatia entered in that way the house of a Croat from Serbia and vice versa and they signed the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, in the village how many Serbs came and how many Croats left? Could you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the territory of the municipality of Sid where I'm from, Kukujevci were not the only village where there was -- where there were Croats. There's Gibarac and Sot. However, we always considered that to be Croat-populated villages before the war and now they are Serb populated, the majority is Serb and there is a very small percentage of Croats. The same thing happened in the town of Sid afterwards as well, people exchanged houses like that neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In figures, how many left? 5? 10? 50? 100? Can you give us a figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how many inhabitants lived in the village of Kukujevci only, for instance. However, I believe that before the war the village of Kukujevci was pretty big and it must have had a population of over 2.000. 90 per cent of all families exchanged houses and went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So 90 per cent of these 2.000 inhabitants left. Apparently 10 per cent stayed. Did any Croats stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, some Croats stayed too. People who were neither Serbs nor Croats stayed too, people who were Slovaks or Ruthenians, but some Croats remained too, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, let's take the situation of a Croat that stays because he does not want to leave for Croatia. How did -- what happened then? Was everything okay or was this person under threat? Was there pressure exerted on this person or did life just go on as it did before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, his old neighbours had left and new neighbours came, people who were Serbs from Croatia with very ugly experience, both of them. But as far as I know it's the police that took care of this. Now, individually what the experiences of all these remaining Croats were, I cannot say. Probably it wasn't very pleasant for them, but later on they probably got used to each other. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: First I want to tender the map that we displayed on the ELMO, it's Exhibit Number 7008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, are you aware of activities by the radicals to intimidate ethnic Croatians in order to encourage them to leave the Vojvodina area?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection. This is a leading question because the Prosecutor is implying that indeed there had been such situations and now she's asking the witness whether he knew about that. First she should ask whether there were such situations, and then if so, whether he knows of any particular examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, be careful when addressing the question and first be very general and go details. If you go into details immediately then it will end up with a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you aware of any activities by members of the Radical Party to encourage Croats to leave the Vojvodina area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about the area of Vojvodina, but I can talk about the territory of my municipality that is in Vojvodina. Certain members of the Serb Radical Party as well as others had certain activities in Kukujevci, Sot, Gibarac. However, these activities quite simply -- well, they went to cafes in some of these villages, sometimes threatened some of these people. Quite simply, the Croats themselves withdrew and created their ghettos in a way. Many armies passed there -- well, I mean, I'm not saying armies, different units were passing there through the village, different people who were resting from the front line in Sid. I know of some cases when people went out and mistreated certain individuals. Sometimes the police did intervene, sometimes they didn't. Now, if a citizen saw himself to be a victim of verbal assault, I don't know whether he'd call the police and then I don't know whether the police reacted. There were such cases. Then there were cases of persons who had already exchanged houses, Serbs who were already living in that village, and there had still been a large number of Croats left and then they contributed to intimidation, as you call it, or whatever, then a lot of the Croats moved out. Well, that is punishable by law, but quite simply no one really paid much attention to that. Somehow all of us in our heart of hearts wanted these Croats to leave. So when we talk about people who behaved in an arrogant manner or committed verbal assaults against Croats, yes, there are members of the Radical Party among them, but others too. And usually say two days after people would hear of an incident, then usually the citizens would always ascribe that to the radicals and I don't know why. In -- it was Milenko Petric who was in the leadership of the Serb Radical Party in Sid at that time. He did not have the capacity of carrying out a selection among his members. All of this in a way got out of control, and I also don't think that there was any channelling in the sense of people directing others to do things like that. Quite simply people would go out and do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to go into private session to ask the next question because I believe it will elicit a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please. [Private session].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as to the time you are asking to get, let me say this in open session. Initially you asked four hours under a Rule 92 ter proceedings. We decided to go for the viva voce testimony. Based on that, we started on Tuesday and you told us you needed eight hours. We said to you, We'll see depending on the beginning of this testimony. You started. After discussing the issue the Judges decided to give you five hours. Therefore, this morning when we started you had already used up three hours. You had two hours left. So in all you've already used four hours and a few minutes. I made a minor mistake thinking that we were finishing by 12.30, but I was wrong. We finish at 1.15, so we've basically got over 45 minutes left. This means that you could finish the examination-in-chief at 1.15 because you would have basically used up your five hours. Of course, granted the Judges put questions. But when we put question it's not sort of debitted from your time. So when I say that you've used up four hours and a few minutes, that's your time, not ours, not mine. As to the time, as per Rules we can control your time. Questions can be -- or requests can be made by the Prosecution, decisions are made by the Judges, because we also have to make sure that we have a speedy trial, that useful questions be put, and we must make sure that we are efficient in the way we manage the trial proceedings. So you basically have nearly 45 minutes left, so please proceed with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me go back into private session then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me restate the question --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was the SCP part of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about the Serbian Chetnik Movement and Mr. Vojislav Seselj and probably a group of his friends, they wanted to register a political party under this name but were unable to, probably because of the name, but the Serbian Chetnik Movement later on when the political party was registered under the name of the Serbian Radical Party according to the statute and all the then-documents I was able to read it was registered as a section of the Serb Radical Party. And in Sid Milenko Petric wanted to register something else, something smaller, to be called the Sokola Association for young people, for children, but I don't know whether this ever happened, whether it ever came to life. But the Chetnik movement was registered as a section of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to look at 65 ter Exhibit Number 83, it's in tab 2 of the Court binder, and I will ask the registrar to give the witness a paper copy in his language.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here what this is, it's the political programme of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were you in 1991 and 1992 familiar with the political platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every office of the Serbian Radical Party, whether in Novi Sad or in Sid, had its library as it was called, various books on book shelves, and these would always include the political programme not only of the Chetnik movement but also of the Serbian Radical Party, the statutes, and so on. And if you wanted to become a member you were able to peruse these books before filling in your application form. I can't say whether I read this in 1991 or 1992. I don't know exactly when I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you look at paragraph 1, please, and read that aloud?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 1: "Renewing the free, independent -- the restoration of a free, independent, and democratic Serbian state in the Balkans which will include all Serbian people and all Serbian territories. Meaning that," it's not very legible here. "In addition to the present Serbian federal unit which has been imposed on us, within its borders it will also include Serbian Macedonia, Serbian Montenegro, Serbian Bosnia, Serbian Herzegovina, Serbian Dubrovnik, Serbian Dalmatia, Serbian Lika, Serbian Kordun, Serbian Banija, Serbian Slavonia, and Serbian Baranja," yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to move the document into evidence or have it identified for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I have an objection. I think this cannot be automatically admitted into evidence without the Prosecutor explaining what sort of document this is. This is a political programme of the Serbian Chetnik Movement before the Serbian Radical Party was founded and it was published in the first issue of the journal Greater Serbia or Velika Srbija in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You gave us information on the background of this document. Could we please have a number because it was not recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, MFI P27.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Judge, one more point, a very important one. The Serbian Radical Party was founded on the 23rd of February, 1991. Should I repeat what I've just said? The Serbian Radical Party was founded on the 23rd of February, 1991, and adopted its programme and statute. It took over all these provisions from the Serbian Chetnik Movement, but this programme was no longer valid because it was replaced by the programme of the Serbian Radical Party from February 1991. The Prosecutor did not say where this document comes from and from what year it dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... we understood. You're saying that the document which is -- has been admitted under the MFI P27 is a document that is earlier -- that was drafted earlier than the radical Serb party that was created on February 23rd, 1991, therefore this document was drafted before the Serbian Radical Party was actually set up. Thank you. Mrs. Dahl could have told us where this document came from. Maybe she went a bit hastily over this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, it's time to finish. As I told you earlier, the three other -- the three Judges must sit on another trial, so what do you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That I'd like to complete the examination tomorrow within the time that you gave me before I understand that you rejected my request for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According -- you have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, I understood that we were finishing at quarter after. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 20 after.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we'll finish at half past or are we going out of session now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Definitely we're going to adjourn because it's time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is -- stops at 1.15. You'll have ten minutes tomorrow morning and then we'll give the floor to Mr. Seselj for his cross-examination. Witness, we will meet again tomorrow at 8.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
